writingIdeas.viewpoint: Green infrastructure should be planned as essential infrastructure.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Urban nature can manage heat and water while improving daily public space.
writingIdeas.argument: A drainage pipe performs one main function, whereas a well-placed rain garden can slow runoff, cool a street and improve the pedestrian environment. These additional benefits justify treating green infrastructure as part of core urban systems rather than optional decoration. However, performance depends on soil, species choice and long-term maintenance, so visual appeal alone is insufficient. Cities should specify measurable functions and fund care from the beginning. When technical and social goals are coordinated, one intervention can solve several local problems.
writingIdeas.viewpointTranslation: 绿色基础设施应作为必要基础设施来规划。
writingIdeas.topicSentenceTranslation: 城市自然可以在改善日常公共空间的同时管理高温和雨水。

argumentSentences.text: These additional benefits justify treating green infrastructure as part of core urban systems rather than optional decoration.

argumentSentences.text: However, performance depends on soil, species choice and long-term maintenance, so visual appeal alone is insufficient.

argumentSentences.text: Cities should specify measurable functions and fund care from the beginning.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Green investment should be directed by need, not available space alone.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Planting where implementation is easiest can reinforce existing inequalities in heat exposure and park access.
writingIdeas.argument: Affluent districts often have wide pavements and mature parks, making additional planting straightforward. Dense lower-income areas may need trees more urgently but require road redesign, utility relocation or land purchase. If planners count only the number planted, they may choose easy sites and miss residents facing the greatest heat risk. Combining temperature data with age, housing and pedestrian routes can identify priority locations. Higher costs in these areas may be justified because equitable planning responds to need rather than distributing identical inputs.
writingIdeas.viewpointTranslation: 绿色投资应依据需求安排，而不只是看哪里有空地。
writingIdeas.topicSentenceTranslation: 只选择最容易实施的地点植树，可能加剧高温暴露和公园使用方面已有的不平等。

speaking.question: Describe a green public space that is useful to local people.
speaking.answer: There is a small park beside a busy shopping street that local people use in several ways. It has mature trees, benches, a drinking fountain and a simple play area, so office workers, parents and older residents all spend time there. I often stop for lunch because the shade makes it noticeably cooler than the surrounding pavement. The park is not large enough for sport, but it connects two pedestrian routes and provides a quiet pause between shops and traffic. What makes it successful is not spectacular landscaping; it is the combination of location, shade and basic facilities. It shows that a modest green space can be valuable when it responds to everyday routines.

speaking.question: What makes an urban green project successful in the long term?
speaking.answer: The design has to suit the site, but maintenance and public use are equally important. A tree species may look attractive yet fail if there is too little soil or no budget for watering during its first years. Residents also need safe routes into the space and reasons to use it at different times. Clear responsibility for pruning, drainage and repairs should be agreed before construction. Finally, success should be measured through shade, biodiversity, water management and access, not just by counting how many plants were installed on opening day.

reading.title: The Unequal Geography of Urban Shade
paragraphs: A city announced that it would plant one hundred thousand trees, presenting the total as both a climate target and a public-health investment. The number was ambitious, but a preliminary map exposed a difficulty: districts with the fewest trees also offered the narrowest pavements, the greatest concentration of underground utilities and the smallest municipal planting budgets. Equal numbers for every district would not produce equal shade.

Tree canopy is usually measured from above, yet residents experience it along particular routes and at particular times. A large private garden can raise a neighbourhood’s canopy percentage without shading a bus stop, while one street tree may protect hundreds of pedestrians during an afternoon heatwave. Planners therefore combined aerial imagery with surface temperatures, walking routes and the locations of schools, clinics and older residents.

The revised programme assigned priority to places where heat exposure and pedestrian use overlapped. In some streets, planting required removing parking spaces and constructing larger soil pits, decisions that were more expensive and politically difficult than adding trees to an existing park. Elsewhere, awnings provided immediate shade while slower-growing trees became established. This mixed approach acknowledged that a planting target, although easy to communicate, was not itself a complete heat strategy.

Maintenance introduced another inequality. Young trees in hotter, paved districts needed more water and were more vulnerable to damage. Funding based only on the number of trees would leave precisely those sites with insufficient care. The city consequently allocated early maintenance according to local growing conditions and published survival rates by district, not merely a citywide total.

Five years is too soon to judge the mature canopy, but it is long enough to learn what survives and whom the programme serves. The initiative still counts trees; counting enables accountability. Its more meaningful question, however, is whether shade appears where people who are most exposed can actually use it. In green urban planning, location, route and time can matter as much as the total visible from the sky.
